▶ I.Overview of Fungi
Core idea: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms that mostly live independently of humans — only a small, specific subset causes disease (mycosis), and how deep they invade determines how mycoses are classified and how serious they are. Page 1–2

A. Classification of Fungi

MUST KNOW
  • Fungi are eukaryotic, nonphotosynthetic, nonmotile, and possess a rigid cell wall. Most are chemotropic — they secrete enzymes to degrade organic matter and absorb the nutrients.
  • Of roughly 80,000 known fungal species, only about 400 are medically relevant, and fewer than 50 species cause >90% of human fungal infections.
  • Fungal disease = mycosis, classified by depth of invasion: superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous, or systemic. This depth reflects not just the site of infection but also the typical route of entry and clinical behavior.
  • Fungi are generally exogenous (natural reservoir = soil, water, decaying matter) except dermatophytes and Candida, which are commensal organisms already adapted to the human host.
  • Th1 and Th17 responses are vital for fungal immunity — this is why opportunistic mycoses are more common in the immunocompromised (chemotherapy, transplant recipients, HIV).
  • Fungi lack potent toxins, unlike many bacteria. Their virulence instead comes from a mix of thermo-tolerance, enzyme secretion, and immune evasion.
  • Drug development is hard because fungi are eukaryotic like human cells and share many biological pathways with us — there are only a limited number of fungus-specific targets.

Classification of Mycoses (Table 1)

Classification of mycoses by depth of invasion
TypeDepthTypical presentation
1. SuperficialOutermost skin layer (stratum corneum) or hair shaftsCosmetic concern more than serious infection
2. CutaneousKeratinized layers — skin, hair, nailsLocalized inflammation, typically dermatophytes
3. SubcutaneousDeeper skin, subcutis, lymphaticsSlow progression, chronic granulomatous inflammation
4. SystemicInternal organsPrimary or opportunistic, mainly in immunocompromised hosts
RECALL CUE
Depth of invasion = S-C-S-S: Superficial (skin surface only) → Cutaneous (skin/hair/nails, keratin) → Subcutaneous (dermis + fat, via trauma) → Systemic (internal organs).

B. Morphologic Forms and Growth

SHOULD KNOW
  • Molds: multicellular, form hyphae → mycelium.
  • Yeasts: unicellular, reproduce by budding ± pseudohyphae.
  • Dimorphic fungi: exist as mold or yeast depending on conditions such as temperature (this becomes critical later for Sporothrix schenckii).
  • Fungal reproduction is asexual (conidia/sporangiospores) or sexual (teleomorphs), aiding dispersal and survival under harsh conditions.
Environmental / room temperature (~25°C)
↓
Mold form — hyphae
Host body temperature (37°C)
↓
Yeast form

This 25°C-mold / 37°C-yeast switch is the definition of thermal dimorphism — keep this pattern in mind, it reappears with Sporothrix schenckii later in the lesson.

C. Cell Wall Components

MUST KNOW Page 2
  • The rigid cell wall provides shape and osmotic protection.
  • Major components: cross-linked polysaccharides — chitin, glucans (β-1,3 and β-1,6), and mannans — plus embedded glycoproteins/lipids (mannoproteins, GPI-anchored proteins).
  • These surface structures mediate adhesion to host tissue, activate innate immunity via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as TLRs, and trigger the complement cascade.
  • Melanin in dematiaceous (darkly pigmented) fungi is built into the cell wall — it provides defense, pigmentation, and enhanced resistance to host immune mechanisms.
DRUG TARGET LINK (from Review Answer Key)
Fungal cell-wall components are the target of major antifungal classes: echinocandins → β-glucan synthesis in the cell wall, while polyenes and azoles → ergosterol / the cell membrane (not the wall itself). This distinction is a favorite exam point.

D. Virulence Factors

MUST KNOW
  • Fungi adapt to the host via morphologic switching (dimorphism) and metabolic reprogramming in response to host signals.
  • Adhesins mediate cellular attachment; enzymes (proteinases, phospholipases) and capsules aid tissue invasion (classic example: Cryptococcus neoformans).
  • Biofilm formation increases resistance to both immunity and drugs.
  • Virulence varies across species/strains and is polygenic — pathogenicity is complex and not attributable to one single factor.
Selected named virulence factors
FactorRole
α-1,3-glucanMasks immunogenic components of the cell wall
MelaninProtects against oxidative stress, imparts dark pigmentation (dematiaceous fungi)
Cryptococcus neoformans capsular polysaccharideInhibits phagocytosis

Taxonomy of Pathogenic Fungi

NICE TO KNOW
  • Modern taxonomy relies on molecular phylogenetics.
  • Major phyla: Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, order Mucorales. Ascomycota makes up >60% of known fungi and ~85% of human fungal pathogens.
  • Reproduction: sexual (teleomorph) via mating-compatible strains, vs. asexual (anamorph), which dominates in clinical specimens and lab culture.
  • ID relies on DNA sequencing, microscopic morphology, and physiologic testing. Many fungi reproduce clonally in the lab, so taxonomic classification often started from the asexual form before a sexual cycle was even discovered.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
Fungi are eukaryotic and DO possess mitochondria, a nucleus, and cell membranes — a classic wrong-answer choice claims otherwise. Fungi are also not photosynthetic.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY — Overview of Fungi
  • <50 species cause >90% of human fungal infections, out of ~80,000 known species.
  • Mycosis classification by depth: superficial → cutaneous → subcutaneous → systemic.
  • Dermatophytes and Candida are the exception to "fungi are exogenous" — they're commensal/endogenous.
  • Th1/Th17 = key protective immune response; opportunistic mycosis ↑ in immunocompromised hosts.
  • Fungi have no potent toxins — virulence = thermotolerance + enzymes + immune evasion (adhesins, capsules, biofilms, melanin).
  • Cell wall = chitin + glucans + mannans; echinocandins hit glucan synthesis, azoles/polyenes hit ergosterol instead.
  • Dimorphic fungi: mold at 25°C (environment), yeast at 37°C (host) — remember this for Sporothrix.
▶ II–III.Fungal Diagnosis & Antifungal Susceptibility Testing
Core idea: Because fungal pathogens and their presentations are so diverse, diagnosis almost always needs more than one method — and once identified, susceptibility testing guides (but does not guarantee) treatment success. Page 2

A. Overview

SHOULD KNOW
  • Fungal infections are typically acquired via environmental exposure (soil, air, water) through traumatic inoculation or mucosal entry.
  • Most fungi are non-contagious, except dermatophytes, which are mildly contagious.
  • Most fungi cannot penetrate intact barriers, but opportunists can still cause severe disease in immunocompromised hosts.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
"Fungi are non-contagious" is the general rule — dermatophytes are the memorable exception and are highly prevalent and contagious (see Cutaneous Mycoses section).

B. Microscopy

MUST KNOW
  • First-line, rapid diagnostic tool for fungal infection.
  • 10–20% KOH prep dissolves host tissue/keratin, highlighting fungal elements (yeast, hyphae, spores).
  • Calcofluor white gives fluorescent enhancement and sensitivity.
  • Special stains: GMS (black), PAS (red), capsule stains.
  • Rapid and cost-effective, but has variable sensitivity.
  • Histopathology uses Gomori methenamine stain / silver (GMS) to visualize fungal elements.

C. Culture

MUST KNOW
  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) is the standard mycology medium — supports fungal growth while suppressing bacteria.
  • Additives: chloramphenicol (antibiotic, suppresses bacteria) and cycloheximide (inhibits contaminating saprophytic fungi) for enhanced selectivity.
  • Yeasts grow at 37°C within days; molds grow at 30°C and can require extended incubation — sometimes several weeks.
  • Culture is more sensitive than microscopy — it's the most sensitive method for diagnosing mycosis overall, but it is slow (days to weeks), and morphology guides species identification.

D. Serology and Molecular Diagnosis

SHOULD KNOW
  • Serology: antibody detection may aid diagnosis in immunocompetent patients; antigen assays (e.g., cryptococcal capsular antigen, 1,3-beta-D-glucan) are used for rapid screening of invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis.
  • PCR-based assays: used for Candida, Aspergillus, and others.
  • MALDI-TOF MS: rapid species-level ID from protein spectra.
  • β-D-glucan assay (Fungitell®): detects fungal polysaccharide.
  • These methods are important adjuncts for early diagnosis of invasive fungal infection.
Clinical suspicion of mycosis → specimen collected (skin scraping, hair, nail, tissue, blood)
↓
Microscopy (KOH / calcofluor white / GMS) — fast, first-line, variable sensitivity
↓
Culture (SDA ± antibiotics) — most sensitive overall, slow (days–weeks)
↓
Serology / molecular assays (antigen, PCR, MALDI-TOF, β-D-glucan) — adjuncts, early ID of invasive disease

III. Antifungal Susceptibility Testing

MUST KNOW
  • MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration) = lowest drug concentration that inhibits fungal growth.
  • CLSI standards define Susceptible, Intermediate, Resistant breakpoints.
  • Most antifungals are fungistatic, not fungicidal — so an MIC result serves as a treatment guide, not a guarantee of clinical success.
  • Commercial kits: Etest® and Sensititre YeastOne®.
  • In vitro susceptibility results may not always correlate with in vivo response.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
A drug being "susceptible" on testing does not mean it will cure the infection — most antifungals only stop growth (fungistatic) rather than kill the organism (fungicidal). Clinical response still depends on host immunity.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY — Diagnosis & Susceptibility Testing
  • Diagnostic hierarchy: Microscopy (fast, first-line) → Culture (most sensitive, slow, gold standard for many) → Serology/molecular (adjunct, early invasive disease).
  • KOH prep 10–20%; calcofluor white fluoresces; GMS = black, PAS = red.
  • SDA ± chloramphenicol (antibacterial) ± cycloheximide (anti-saprophyte).
  • Yeasts: 37°C, days. Molds: 30°C, weeks.
  • MIC/CLSI breakpoints guide therapy but most antifungals are only fungistatic.
▶ IV.Superficial Mycoses
Core idea: All three superficial mycoses stay in the outermost dead skin/hair layer — minimal inflammation, mostly a cosmetic issue, and each has its own classic microscopy "buzzword." Pages 2–3

A. Malassezia furfur — Tinea (Pityriasis) Versicolor

MUST KNOW
  • Common, chronic superficial mycosis, caused by Malassezia globosa, M. furfur, M. sympodialis.
  • This is a lipophilic yeast that is part of the normal cutaneous flora — making the infection endogenous.
  • Presents as hyper/hypopigmented macules on the trunk (chest and back) and arms. Lesions may coalesce but show minimal inflammation.
  • Diagnosis: KOH prep shows short unbranched hyphae + round yeast — described as "spaghetti and meatballs." Wood's lamp gives positive fluorescence.
  • Treatment aims to reduce fungal load, not eradicate the organism (it's normal flora) — selenium sulfide or topical/oral azoles.
RECALL CUE
"Spaghetti and meatballs" on KOH = Malassezia furfur (tinea versicolor). This is the single most quoted buzzword for superficial mycoses.

B. Hortaea werneckii — Tinea Nigra

SHOULD KNOW
  • Superficial, asymptomatic infection caused by Hortaea werneckii, a dematiaceous (pigmented) fungus.
  • Appears as a dark macule on palms/soles — can be mistaken for a pigmented lesion.
  • Microscopy: branched septate hyphae, pigmented yeast.
  • Treatment: salicylic acid (keratolytic agent), topical azoles.

C. Piedra

SHOULD KNOW
  • Nodular infection of the hair shaft, common in tropical climates.
  • Black piedra — caused by Piedraia hortae — a hard, black nodule.
  • White piedra — caused by Trichosporon species — softer, yellowish nodules.
  • Hair from the scalp, axilla, beard, or pubic region may be affected.
  • Treatment: mechanical removal of infected hair + topical antifungal.
Do not confuse: White Piedra vs. Black Piedra
White Piedra
Organism: Trichosporon spp.
Nodule: soft, yellowish, easily removable
Black Piedra
Organism: Piedraia hortae
Nodule: hard, black, firm/adherent
Fast distinction: Color and hardness tell you the organism — black & hard = Piedraia; white & soft = Trichosporon.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY — Superficial Mycoses
  • Malassezia furfur → tinea versicolor → hyper/hypopigmented trunk macules → "spaghetti and meatballs" on KOH → selenium sulfide/azoles (reduce load, don't eradicate — it's normal flora).
  • Hortaea werneckii → tinea nigra → dark palm/sole macule, dematiaceous, asymptomatic.
  • Piedraia hortae → black piedra (hard, black). Trichosporon → white piedra (soft, yellow).
  • All three stay confined to the outermost skin/hair layer — minimal to no inflammation, mostly cosmetic.
▶ V.Cutaneous Mycoses — Dermatophytosis
Core idea: Dermatophytes infect only keratin (skin, hair, nails) because they cannot survive at 37°C — so infections are superficial and chronic, never invasive, but they are the one truly contagious group of fungi. Pages 3–5

A. Overview of Dermatophytosis

MUST KNOW
  • Cutaneous fungal infection restricted to keratinized tissues: skin, hair, and nails.
  • Caused by ~40 related fungi in three genera: Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton.
  • Dermatophytes cannot grow at 37°C → confined to nonviable superficial layers → infections are superficial, often chronic but not severe or life-threatening.
  • Among the most common mycoses worldwide; may be persistent or recurrent.
  • Transmitted through contact with infected people, infected animals, contaminated soil, or fomites.
  • Highly prevalent and contagious — this makes dermatophytes unique, since most other fungal infections are non-communicable.

Predisposing factors: hot/humid climate, skin trauma, moisture, genetic susceptibility, impaired immunity.

⚠ EXAM TRAP
Dermatophytes are the exception that proves the rule — while most fungi are non-contagious, dermatophytes spread person-to-person, animal-to-person, and via fomites (towels, combs, gym mats).

B. Dermatophyte Genera and Morphology

MUST KNOW
The three dermatophyte genera
GenusInfectsConidia producedNotes
TrichophytonSkin, hair, nailsNumerous microconidia + occasional smooth-walled macroconidiaGlobally distributed: T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes
MicrosporumSkin, hair (not nails)Large, thick-walled, multicellular macroconidia (rough/curved/hooked ends)—
Epidermophyton floccosumSkin, nails (not hair)Club-shaped/clavate, smooth-walled macroconidia; no microconidiaOnly pathogenic species in its genus
RECALL CUE
Only Trichophyton hits all three (skin + hair + nails). Microsporum skips nails. Epidermophyton skips hair.

Lab cultivation: grown on Sabouraud dextrose agar, incubated at 25–30°C. Species ID relies on colony morphology, microscopic appearance, type/arrangement of conidia, and PCR.

C. Morphologic Features of Dermatophytes

SHOULD KNOW Page 3, Table 3
  • T. tonsurans: numerous elongated microconidia attached to supporting hyphae.
  • M. gypseum: numerous, individual, thin- and rough-walled macroconidia.
  • E. floccosum: club-shaped, thin- and smooth-walled macroconidia, typically in small clusters.

D. Epidemiology and Host Response

MUST KNOW
Ecological niche and resulting clinical response
Ecological categorySourceClinical response
AnthropophilicAdapted to humansMild, chronic, low-grade infection — responsible for most human cases
ZoophilicAnimals (e.g., pets)Acute, inflammatory reaction — may occasionally resolve spontaneously
GeophilicSoilAcute, inflammatory reaction — may occasionally resolve spontaneously

Modes of transmission: direct skin-to-skin contact, contact with infected animals, contact with contaminated objects/fomites (clothing, towels, combs, gym mats).
Host factors: genetics, immune status — some individuals show IgE-mediated hypersensitivity with a poor cell-mediated immune response, which worsens disease persistence.

RECALL CUE
Anthropophilic = Adapted to us = mild/chronic. Zoophilic/Geophilic = "outsider" strains = more acute/inflammatory (and may self-resolve).

E. Dermatophytosis: Clinical Forms

MUST KNOW
  • "Tinea/Ringworm" is the historical name, classified and named by anatomical location.
  • "Ringworm" refers to the linear, raised, annular appearance of the lesion — it is not caused by an actual worm.
  • The same fungal species can produce multiple clinical forms, and a single clinical form may be caused by several different dermatophyte species.
  • Typical lesion: pruritic, annular patch with an active, raised erythematous margin, peripheral scaling, and central clearing.
  • Inflammatory response again tracks ecological source: anthropophilic = mild/chronic; zoophilic/geophilic = more acute/inflammatory.
  • Diagnosis: KOH microscopy, fungal culture, Wood's lamp (especially useful for certain Microsporum infections).
⚠ EXAM TRAP / CLINICAL PEARL
"Ringworm" describes the ring-shaped appearance of the lesion — it is not caused by an actual worm.
Clinical forms named by anatomical site
SiteName
FeetTinea pedis
NailsTinea unguium (onychomycosis)
GroinTinea cruris
HandsTinea manuum
Scalp and hairTinea capitis
Beard and mustache areaTinea barbae
Glabrous (hairless) body skinTinea corporis

01 | Tinea Pedis (athlete's foot)

MUST KNOW
  • Most prevalent form of dermatophytosis; not limited to athletes. Commonly begins in the interdigital spaces/toe webs.
  • Clinical: scaling, peeling, maceration, fissures; possible secondary bacterial infection in chronic cases.
  • Variants: interdigital, moccasin-type (plantar hyperkeratosis), vesicular (blistering), ulcerative.
  • Repeatedly wet feet increase the risk — especially relevant during flooding.

02 | Tinea Unguium / Onychomycosis

MUST KNOW
  • Occurs when dermatophyte infection involves the nails.
  • Produces nails that are thickened, discolored/yellow, brittle, friable.
CLINICAL PEARL
Tinea pedis affects the feet; tinea unguium affects the nails and usually needs longer treatment.

03 | Tinea Corporis

MUST KNOW
  • "Ringworm of the body" — classic ringworm on glabrous/relatively hairless skin.
  • Erythematous advancing border, peripheral scaling, central clearing, active margin.

04 | Tinea Cruris ("jock itch")

MUST KNOW
  • Common among adult males; affects the groin and upper inner thighs.
  • Starts in the scrotum, then spreads to the groin and thighs.
  • Lesions: dry, pruritic, sharply demarcated.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
Classic tinea cruris mainly involves the groin and upper inner thighs. Prominent scrotal involvement usually suggests an alternative diagnosis, such as candidiasis — not tinea cruris.

05 | Tinea Manus / Manuum

SHOULD KNOW
  • Affects hands, palms, or fingers; produces dry, scaly plaques.
  • May be asymmetrical, affecting only one hand.
BUZZWORD (from lecturer's Appendix table)
"Two feet–one hand" syndrome — chronic T. rubrum tinea pedis on both feet with tinea manuum affecting only one hand.

06 | Tinea Capitis

MUST KNOW Page 5
  • Dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair; occurs most commonly in children.
  • Ectothrix infection: arthroconidia/spores located outside the hair shaft, commonly associated with Microsporum species, infected hairs may fluoresce green under Wood's lamp.
  • Endothrix infection: arthroconidia/spores located inside the hair shaft, seen with organisms such as Trichophyton tonsurans, infected hairs do not fluoresce.
  • Severe inflammatory responses: Kerion (painful, boggy, inflammatory scalp lesion; zoophilic) and Favus (chronic infection with yellowish crusts/scutula; zoophilic).
IMPORTANT TO KNOW
Ectothrix: spores outside the hair shaft = may fluoresce under Wood's lamp.
Endothrix: spores inside the hair shaft = does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp.

07 | Tinea Barbae

SHOULD KNOW
  • Dermatophyte infection of the beard and mustache area; occurs in adult males.
  • Frequently presents as an inflammatory lesion that may resemble bacterial folliculitis — proper diagnosis is necessary to distinguish the two.

F. Trichophytid Reaction

SHOULD KNOW
  • Hypersensitivity response to dermatophyte antigens, occurring during an active dermatophyte infection elsewhere in the body.
  • Commonly presents as a vesicular eruption on the hands, distant from the primary site of infection.
  • Reflects immune sensitization, not direct fungal invasion — commonly associated with a positive trichophytin skin test.
  • May resolve after treatment of the primary fungal infection.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
Trichophytid reaction is a hypersensitivity reaction, not direct fungal spread to the hands. The distant eruption clears once the primary infection is treated — no fungus is actually growing at that distant site.

G. Dermatophytosis: Laboratory Diagnosis

MUST KNOW
  • Specimens: skin scrapings, nail clippings, infected hairs.
  • KOH prep dissolves keratin and reveals branching, septate hyphae and chains of arthroconidia.
Dermatophyte invades a hair shaft
Ectothrix → arthroconidia form dense external sheets around the hair shaft → seen with Microsporum → hair fluoresces green
Endothrix → arthroconidia located within the hair shaft → seen with Trichophyton tonsurans → no fluorescence

H. Dermatophyte Culture

SHOULD KNOW
  • Media: Inhibitory mold agar (IMA), SDA ± cycloheximide (inhibits saprophytic contaminants) ± chloramphenicol (suppresses bacteria).
  • Incubated at room temperature; growth usually requires ~1–3 weeks.
  • Species identification uses macroscopic colony morphology (texture, color, growth rate), microscopic characteristics (conidia type/arrangement, macro- vs. microconidia), and additional tests (nutritional/growth-requirement tests, hair-perforation test).

I. Treatment of Dermatophytosis

MUST KNOW
  • General management: debride infected/nonviable tissue when appropriate; maintain a dry environment to prevent persistence/recurrence.
  • Topical antifungals (miconazole, tolnaftate, clotrimazole) are generally sufficient for mild, localized infection (tinea corporis, mild tinea pedis). Apply for at least 2–4 weeks, and continue for 1–2 weeks after symptoms resolve.
  • Oral antifungals (griseofulvin, terbinafine, itraconazole) are required for extensive infection, persistent/refractory infection, tinea capitis, and tinea unguium.
  • Site-specific notes: Tinea capitis requires oral treatment (frequent shampooing may be added). Tinea unguium is particularly resistant to treatment, may require several months of oral therapy, and surgical nail removal may sometimes be necessary — luliconazole has shown promise because it penetrates the nail bed.
Mild, localized (tinea corporis / mild tinea pedis)
↓
Topical antifungal — 2–4 wks, continue 1–2 wks after symptoms resolve
Extensive / persistent / scalp / nail involvement
↓
Oral antifungal (griseofulvin, terbinafine, itraconazole) ± shampoo (capitis) / nail removal (unguium)
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY — Cutaneous Mycoses / Dermatophytosis
  • Three genera: Trichophyton (skin+hair+nails), Microsporum (skin+hair, no nails), Epidermophyton (skin+nails, no hair, no microconidia).
  • Dermatophytes can't grow at 37°C → superficial and chronic, never systemic, but they are contagious — the exception among fungi.
  • Anthropophilic = mild/chronic; Zoophilic/Geophilic = acute/inflammatory (may self-resolve).
  • "Ringworm" = shape of the lesion, not an actual worm.
  • Ectothrix (outside hair, Microsporum, fluoresces) vs. Endothrix (inside hair, T. tonsurans, no fluorescence).
  • Tinea cruris with prominent scrotal involvement → think candidiasis, not tinea.
  • Trichophytid reaction = hypersensitivity, not direct fungal spread.
  • Topical for mild/localized disease; oral (griseofulvin/terbinafine/itraconazole) for extensive disease, tinea capitis, or tinea unguium.
▶ VI.Subcutaneous Mycoses
Core idea: All three subcutaneous mycoses (sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, mycetoma) get in the same way — traumatic inoculation from soil or plant material — but each has its own hallmark tissue finding and clinical picture. Pages 6–8

A. Overview

MUST KNOW
  • Acquired through traumatic inoculation into the dermis/subcutaneous tissue.
  • Infections are typically chronic, slowly progressive, and granulomatous; some form draining sinuses.
  • Lymphatic spread is characteristic of certain infections, particularly sporotrichosis.
  • Systemic dissemination is rare, but may occur in immunocompromised individuals.

B. Sporotrichosis

MUST KNOW
  • Subcutaneous mycosis caused by thermally dimorphic fungi of the genus Sporothrix (S. schenckii complex). Important species: S. brasiliensis (zoonotic cases), S. globosa (may cause non-lymphatic forms).
  • Usually acquired through traumatic implantation from soil or plant material. Environmental sources: soil, sphagnum moss, plants, rose bushes.
  • Commonly produces nodular lesions that spread along the lymphatic vessels.
25°C / room temperature
↓
Mold phase — septate hyphae with delicate, pear-shaped (piriform) conidia
37°C / human tissue
↓
Yeast phase — small, cigar-shaped budding yeast cells (3–5 μm)

Initial diagnostic methods: fungal culture, histopathologic examination, serologic testing; delayed skin testing using heat-killed sporotrichin antigen may support the diagnosis.

Clinical Features (Table 4)

MUST KNOW
Clinical forms of sporotrichosis
FormFeatures
Lymphocutaneous
(~75% of cases)		Most common form. Begins as a granulomatous skin nodule at the inoculation site → ulceration → spreads along draining lymphatic channels, producing a cord-like pattern with multiple subcutaneous nodules/abscesses.
Fixed cutaneousSingle, localized lesion. Does not spread along lymphatics. More common in endemic areas with high exposure.
DisseminatedSystemic dissemination is uncommon; may occur in debilitated/immunocompromised patients.
PulmonaryRare; may clinically resemble tuberculosis.

Risk factors: trauma during gardening, farming, or floristry; exposure to rose thorns, sphagnum moss, or contaminated plant material.

Diagnostic Laboratory Tests

MUST KNOW
  • Specimens: biopsy material, aspirate/exudate from lesions.
  • Direct microscopy (KOH/calcofluor white): yeast forms are usually sparse and hard to visualize — often negative even with true infection.
  • Histopathology: GMS stain → fungal walls appear black; PAS stain → fungal walls appear red/magenta. Look for cigar-shaped yeast cells and asteroid bodies surrounding yeast cells.
  • Culture = gold standard for diagnosis — grown on inhibitory mold agar or SDA at 25–30°C, confirmed by conversion to the yeast phase at ~35–37°C.
  • Serology is not routinely recommended — limited by inadequate specificity/sensitivity, with false-positive and false-negative results.
IMPORTANT TO KNOW
Culture is the gold standard for diagnosing sporotrichosis. Direct microscopy may be negative because yeast cells are usually sparse in tissue.

Morphology and Identification

SHOULD KNOW
  • Mold phase (25°C): grows on glucose agar/SDA; colony starts light-colored, turns brown to black as melanin accumulates; septate hyphae produce pear-shaped (piriform) conidia arranged along the hyphae sides or in rosette/flower-like clusters.
  • Yeast phase (37°C): grown on brain–heart infusion agar; shows budding yeast and the classic cigar-shaped yeast cells.
  • Lab ID: lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) stain shows mold structures/conidial arrangement; demonstrating thermal dimorphism supports the diagnosis.

Treatment, Prevention & Transmission

MUST KNOW
  • Some localized cases may be self-limited.
  • Itraconazole = drug of choice for most cutaneous and lymphocutaneous cases.
  • Saturated solution of potassium iodide (SSKI): older alternative, effective but frequently poorly tolerated.
  • Amphotericin B: indicated for systemic, disseminated, or severe disease.
NICE TO KNOW
  • Prevention: reduce exposure to contaminated soil/plant material; wear protective gloves, long sleeves, protective clothing; exercise caution around rose thorns, sphagnum moss, decaying wood. Agricultural/horticultural workers are at increased risk.
  • Transmission: zoonotic transmission is possible from infected animals; veterinary precautions may be necessary.

C. Chromoblastomycosis

MUST KNOW Pages 7–8
  • Chronic subcutaneous infection caused by dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi, acquired through traumatic implantation of fungi from soil or vegetation.
  • Produces a verrucous, granulomatous lesion at the site of inoculation, with marked epidermal hyperplasia.
  • Common etiologic agents: Phialophora verrucosa, Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Fonsecaea compacta, Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, Cladophialophora carrionii.
IMPORTANT TO KNOW
Chromoblastomycosis results from pigmented fungi introduced by traumatic implantation.

Morphology and Identification

SHOULD KNOW
  • Culture appearance: compact, velvety or wrinkled, deep brown to black colonies — dark color from melanin production.
  • Tissue morphology — the key diagnostic finding: the muriform or sclerotic body (also called Medlar body or copper penny body). Appears as a thick-walled, brown, spherical fungal cell, 4–12 μm, with transverse and longitudinal septations.
  • Identification by conidial structure (detailed arrangements do not need to be memorized per the lecturer): Phialophora verrucosa (cup-shaped collarettes), Fonsecaea pedrosoi (polymorphic, multiple conidiation modes), Fonsecaea compacta (spherical blastoconidia, broad base), Rhinocladiella aquaspersa (sympodial elliptical conidia), Cladophialophora carrionii (long branching chains of oval conidia).
IMPORTANT TO KNOW
The important diagnostic tissue finding in chromoblastomycosis is the muriform or sclerotic body.

Clinical Features and Pathogenesis

MUST KNOW
Traumatic implantation (often legs/feet of barefoot agricultural workers)
↓
Early lesion: slowly enlarging papule/nodule at the inoculation site
↓
Typical appearance: warty / verrucous, cauliflower-like — may develop crusting, abscesses, ulceration, black dots
↓
Chronic, slowly progressive — lesions enlarge; lymphatic obstruction may cause elephantiasis
↓
Satellite lesions (lymphatic spread or autoinoculation) — systemic dissemination is rare

Diagnosis

MUST KNOW
  • KOH prep: demonstrates muriform/sclerotic bodies — diagnostic of chromoblastomycosis.
  • Histopathology: epidermal hyperplasia, granulomatous inflammation, intracellular muriform cells.
  • Culture: on IMA or SDA with antibiotics — produces dark green, brown, or black colonies; species differentiated by growth and conidial structure.
CLINICAL PEARL
A chronic, warty lesion containing brown muriform bodies on KOH examination strongly indicates chromoblastomycosis.

Treatment, Epidemiology & Prevention

SHOULD KNOW
  • Surgical excision: preferred for small, localized lesions.
  • Itraconazole or flucytosine: used for larger/extensive lesions.
  • Local heat therapy may assist; treatment frequently requires prolonged follow-up and relapse is common.
NICE TO KNOW
  • Occurs mainly in tropical climates; organisms found in soil/vegetation; most common among agricultural workers; barefoot workers have ↑ risk. Not transmitted person-to-person.
  • Prevention: protective footwear/clothing, avoid direct soil/vegetation trauma, clean and manage wounds promptly.

D. Mycetoma

MUST KNOW Page 8–9
  • Chronic granulomatous infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, acquired through traumatic implantation of soil-dwelling organisms.
  • May be caused by true fungi (Eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria/actinomycetes (Actinomycetoma).
  • Classical triad: localized swelling + multiple draining sinuses/fistulae + granules containing colonies of the causative organism.
IMPORTANT TO KNOW
MYCETOMA TRIAD — Localized swelling + draining sinuses + granules.
⚠ EXAM TRAP
Actinomycetoma is caused by filamentous bacteria, not fungi, and is explicitly not included in this fungal discussion — don't let the name "myceto-" trick you into calling it a fungal infection.

Morphology and Identification

SHOULD KNOW
  • Common fungal agents: Pseudallescheria boydii (also called Scedosporium apiospermum), Madurella mycetomatis, Madurella grisea, Exophiala jeanselmei, Acremonium falciforme.
  • Granules vary in color, size, and texture — these characteristics help identify the causative organism:
    • White granules → suggest Pseudallescheria boydii
    • Black to red-black granules → suggest Madurella or Exophiala
  • Microscopically, granules contain densely intertwined septate hyphae, often distorted at the periphery; hyphae ~3–5 μm; granules ~2 mm, firm and difficult to fragment.

Pathogenesis and Clinical Features

MUST KNOW
Trauma introduces fungal spores from contaminated soil/plant material into the skin
↓
Chronic infection: suppurative inflammation → granuloma formation → draining sinus tracts → discharge with fungal granules

Common sites: feet, hands, lower limbs. Progression: infection may extend into muscle/bone; untreated disease may cause deformity, disability, functional loss. Systemic dissemination is uncommon (may occur in immunocompromised patients).

Diagnosis & Treatment

SHOULD KNOW
  • Diagnosis: obtain granules from pus/sinus discharge or tissue biopsy; examine with KOH prep; culture on SDA or inhibitory mold agar; identify by granule color, granule size/consistency, hyphal morphology, and culture characteristics.
  • Treatment: difficult and often prolonged — usually a combination of surgical excision/debridement plus long-term antifungal therapy (itraconazole, ketoconazole, amphotericin B). Specific treatment depends on the causative species.
NICE TO KNOW
  • Prevention: protective footwear (especially in endemic regions), proper wound hygiene, prompt wound care after trauma, prevent direct inoculation of contaminated soil/plant material.
HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY — Subcutaneous Mycoses
  • All three enter via traumatic inoculation from soil/plant material and are typically chronic, slow, granulomatous, with rare systemic spread.
  • Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix, dimorphic): lymphocutaneous form (75%) spreads along lymphatics → cord-like nodules. Hallmark: cigar-shaped yeast + asteroid bodies. Culture = gold standard (microscopy often falsely negative — sparse yeast). Itraconazole = DOC; amphotericin B for severe/disseminated disease.
  • Chromoblastomycosis (dematiaceous fungi, e.g. Fonsecaea pedrosoi): verrucous, cauliflower-like lesion. Hallmark: muriform/sclerotic (Medlar/copper-penny) body on KOH. Surgery for small lesions; itraconazole/flucytosine for larger ones; relapse common.
  • Mycetoma (true fungi = eumycetoma; bacteria = actinomycetoma — not covered here): classic triad = swelling + draining sinuses + granules. Granule color is a clue: white → Pseudallescheria boydii; black/red-black → Madurella/Exophiala.

⚠ EXAM TRAP — Video vs. Book Classification Discrepancy (from the trans Appendix)
The classifications of diseases and causative organisms in the lecture video and in Jawetz (28th ed.) are switched. For example: in the video, Malassezia furfur is classified as cutaneous and Trichophyton rubrum is classified as superficial — the opposite of the book. This reviewer (and the master tables above) follow the book/Jawetz convention used in the main body of this trans: Malassezia furfur = superficial, dermatophytes (T. rubrum, etc.) = cutaneous. If an exam question is drawn directly from the lecture video, remember the labels for these two organisms specifically may be swapped.
▶ Commonly Confused Concepts
Do not confuse: Ectothrix vs. Endothrix
Ectothrix
Arthroconidia outside the hair shaft
Classic organism: Microsporum
Hair may fluoresce green under Wood's lamp
Endothrix
Arthroconidia inside the hair shaft
Classic organism: Trichophyton tonsurans
Hair does not fluoresce
Fast distinction: If it glows green, it's outside (ecto-); if it's dark under the lamp, it's inside (endo-).
Do not confuse: White Piedra vs. Black Piedra
White Piedra
Trichosporon spp.
Soft, yellowish, easily removed nodules
Black Piedra
Piedraia hortae
Hard, black, firmly adherent nodules
Fast distinction: Texture and color point straight to the organism.
Do not confuse: Anthropophilic vs. Zoophilic vs. Geophilic Dermatophytes
Anthropophilic
Adapted to humans
Responsible for most human cases
Mild, chronic disease
Zoophilic / Geophilic
From animals / soil
Acute, inflammatory reaction
May occasionally resolve spontaneously
Fast distinction: The more "foreign" the source, the more inflamed (and shorter-lived) the reaction tends to be.
Do not confuse: Malassezia furfur / T. rubrum — Video vs. Book Classification
Book (Jawetz) / this trans's main text
Malassezia furfur → superficial
Trichophyton rubrum → cutaneous
Lecture video (per Appendix note)
Malassezia furfur → cutaneous
Trichophyton rubrum → superficial
Fast distinction: This reviewer follows the book convention throughout — but know that the two sources disagree specifically on these two organisms.
Do not confuse: Lymphocutaneous vs. Fixed Cutaneous Sporotrichosis
Lymphocutaneous (~75%)
Spreads along lymphatic channels
Cord-like nodules/abscesses
Fixed cutaneous
Single, localized lesion
No lymphatic spread
Fast distinction: Does it march up the limb in a line, or stay put? Marching = lymphocutaneous.
Do not confuse: Sporotrichosis vs. Chromoblastomycosis vs. Mycetoma
Sporotrichosis
Dimorphic yeast
Cord-like nodules
Cigar-shaped yeast + asteroid bodies
Chromoblastomycosis
Dematiaceous mold
Cauliflower-like plaque
Muriform/sclerotic bodies
Mycetoma
True fungi or bacteria
Swelling + sinuses + granules (triad)
Granule color IDs the organism
Fast distinction: All three enter by trauma — but the hallmark microscopic finding is different for each, and only mycetoma has visible granules draining from sinus tracts.
Do not confuse: Eumycetoma vs. Actinomycetoma
Eumycetoma
Caused by true fungi (e.g., Madurella, Pseudallescheria)
Actinomycetoma
Caused by filamentous bacteria
Not covered in this fungal lecture
Fast distinction: Same clinical triad, different kingdom of organism entirely.
Do not confuse: Trichophytid Reaction vs. Direct Dermatophyte Invasion
Trichophytid reaction
Hypersensitivity to antigens
Vesicles appear distant from the real infection
No fungus actually there
Direct invasion
Active fungal growth at the site
KOH/culture positive at that site
Fast distinction: A trichophytid eruption resolves once the real (distant) infection is treated — you never find fungus in the vesicles themselves.
Do not confuse: Culture vs. Microscopy (sensitivity vs. speed)
Microscopy (KOH)
Fast, first-line
Variable sensitivity
Culture
Slow (days–weeks)
Most sensitive — gold standard for many mycoses
Fast distinction: Order matters clinically — do KOH first for a fast answer, but don't rule a mycosis out until culture is back (especially for sporotrichosis, where yeast forms are often too sparse to see directly).
Do not confuse: Fungistatic vs. Fungicidal
Fungistatic
Stops growth — most antifungals fall here
Fungicidal
Kills the organism outright — the exception, not the rule, for antifungals
Fast distinction: "Susceptible" on an MIC panel only means the drug can stop growth at that concentration — it does not promise a fungicidal cure.
▶ Exam Traps — Compiled

These traps also appear inline within their topic sections — they're gathered here for a fast, final pass.

⚠ 1. "Ringworm" is a misnomer
The linear, raised, annular lesion shape gives dermatophytosis its historical name — there is no actual worm involved.
⚠ 2. Fungi are generally non-contagious — except dermatophytes
Most mycoses are acquired from the environment and are not spread person-to-person. Dermatophytes are the memorable exception: they are highly prevalent and contagious.
⚠ 3. Prominent scrotal involvement in a groin rash ≠ tinea cruris
Classic tinea cruris spares the scrotum. If the scrotum is prominently involved, think candidiasis instead.
⚠ 4. Trichophytid reaction is hypersensitivity, not fungal invasion
The vesicular eruption on the hands is immune-mediated and appears distant from the actual infection — it is not itself infected tissue.
⚠ 5. A "susceptible" MIC result does not guarantee a cure
Most antifungals are fungistatic, not fungicidal — in vitro susceptibility may not correlate with in vivo clinical response.
⚠ 6. Serology is not reliable for sporotrichosis
It is not routinely recommended due to inadequate specificity/sensitivity and both false-positive and false-negative results. Culture remains the gold standard.
⚠ 7. Actinomycetoma is bacterial, not fungal
Despite the name "myceto-," actinomycetoma is caused by filamentous bacteria and is explicitly excluded from this fungal lecture. Only eumycetoma (true fungi) is covered here.
⚠ 8. The lecture video and Jawetz (book) swap two classifications
Malassezia furfur and Trichophyton rubrum are classified oppositely (superficial vs. cutaneous) between the video and the textbook. This reviewer follows the book/main-trans convention.
⚠ 9. Zoophilic/geophilic infections can resolve on their own
Despite being more acutely inflammatory, these infections "may occasionally resolve spontaneously" — don't assume acute automatically means it requires more aggressive treatment than a chronic anthropophilic infection.
⚠ 10. Direct microscopy can be falsely negative in sporotrichosis
Yeast forms are usually sparse in tissue — a negative KOH/calcofluor does not rule out sporotrichosis. Culture is required to confirm.
⚠ 11. Fungi are eukaryotic and do have mitochondria
A classic wrong-answer choice claims fungi lack mitochondria, a nucleus, or cell membranes — all of these are present. Fungi are also not photosynthetic.
⚠ 12. Cell wall components are not the same as cell membrane components
Echinocandins target the cell wall (β-glucan synthesis); polyenes and azoles target the cell membrane (ergosterol). Don't mix these two structures up when matching drug class to target.
▶ Review Questions (from Jawetz, Ch. 45)

The 7 questions printed at the end of the trans, with the answer key. Tap a question to reveal the answer and explanation.

1. Which statement regarding fungi is correct?
a. All fungi are able to grow as yeasts and molds
b. Although fungi are eukaryotes, they lack mitochondria
c. Fungi are photosynthetic
d. Fungi have one or more nuclei and chromosomes ✓
e. Few fungi possess cell membranes
Why: Fungi are eukaryotic organisms and possess cell membranes, mitochondria, nuclei, and chromosomes.
2. Which statement regarding fungal growth and morphology is correct?
a. Pseudohyphae are produced by all yeasts
b. Molds produce hyphae that may or may not be partitioned with cross-walls or septa ✓
c. Conidia are produced by sexual reproduction
d. Most pathogenic dimorphic molds produce hyphae in the host and yeasts at 30°C
e. Most pathogenic dimorphic molds produce hyphae in the host and yeasts at 0°C
Why: Molds grow as hyphae, which can be either septate or nonseptate (coenocytic). Pseudohyphae are not produced by all yeasts, and conidia are asexual reproductive structures. Classic dimorphic fungi generally grow as molds at lower temperatures and as yeast-like forms at body temperature.
3. Which statement regarding fungal cell walls is correct?
a. The major components of fungal cell walls are proteins such as chitin, glucans, and mannans
b. The cell wall is not essential for fungal viability or survival
c. Ligands associated with the cell walls of certain fungi mediate attachment to host cells ✓
d. Fungal cell wall components are the targets for the major classes of antifungal antibiotics, such as the polyenes and azoles
e. Fungal cell wall components rarely stimulate an immune response
Why: Certain fungal cell-wall components function as adhesins, facilitating attachment to host cells/tissues. Chitin, glucans, and mannans are carbohydrates, not proteins. Polyenes and azoles primarily target the cell membrane/ergosterol, while echinocandins target fungal cell-wall glucan synthesis.
4. A 54-year-old man develops a slowly worsening headache and progressive right-arm weakness. A brain scan reveals a left cerebral lesion. Surgery finds an abscess surrounded by granulomatous material, with darkly pigmented septate hyphae indicating phaeohyphomycosis. This infection may be caused by species of which genus?
a. Aspergillus
b. Cladophialophora ✓
c. Coccidioides
d. Malassezia
e. Sporothrix
Why: Cladophialophora is a dematiaceous (darkly pigmented) fungus associated with phaeohyphomycosis, particularly cerebral infection and brain abscesses. The key words are darkly pigmented, septate hyphae.
5. A 35-year-old farmer in tropical West Africa develops a persistent scaly papule, followed ten months later by wart-like purplish lesions that slowly become cauliflower-like. Chromoblastomycosis is diagnosed. Which statement is most correct?
a. In tissue, the organisms convert to spherical cells that reproduce by fission and exhibit transverse septations ✓
b. The etiologic agents are endogenous members of the mammalian flora and possess melanized cell walls
c. The disease is caused by a single species
d. Most infections are systemic
e. Most infections are acute and clear spontaneously
Why: Chromoblastomycosis is characterized histologically by sclerotic (Medlar/muriform) bodies — thick-walled, brown, spherical cells with transverse and longitudinal septations. It is a chronic, localized subcutaneous infection caused by several dematiaceous fungi, commonly acquired through traumatic inoculation in tropical or rural environments.
6. An 8-year-old boy develops a circular, dry, scaly, pruritic leg lesion. What is the diagnostic significance of branching, septate, nonpigmented hyphae on a KOH/calcofluor white prep of a scraping?
a. Chromoblastomycosis
b. Dermatophytosis ✓
c. Phaeohyphomycosis
d. Sporotrichosis
e. No diagnostic significance
Why: Dermatophytes characteristically produce hyaline, branching, septate hyphae, readily demonstrated with KOH or calcofluor white. The circular, dry, scaly, pruritic lesion is typical of tinea corporis.
7. Which statement regarding dermatophytosis is correct?
a. Chronic infections are associated with zoophilic dermatophytes, such as M. canis
b. Chronic infections are associated with anthropophilic dermatophytes, such as M. canis ✓
c. Acute infections are associated with anthropophilic dermatophytes, such as M. canis
d. Acute infections are associated with zoophilic dermatophytes, such as M. canis
Why: Anthropophilic dermatophytes are adapted to humans and typically cause chronic, less inflammatory infections.
▶ Cram Sheet (5–10 Minute Read)

A complete, condensed run-through of the whole lesson. Nothing new here — just the highest-yield facts pulled together.

1.Depth of invasion classifies mycoses: superficial (stratum corneum/hair) → cutaneous (skin+hair+nails) → subcutaneous (dermis/subcutis, via trauma) → systemic (internal organs).
2.Only <50 fungal species cause >90% of human infections. Dermatophytes and Candida are the exception to "fungi are exogenous" — they're commensal.
3.Fungi have no potent toxins. Virulence = thermotolerance + enzymes + immune evasion (adhesins, capsules, biofilm, melanin). Th1/Th17 are the key protective immune responses.
4.Cell wall = chitin + β-glucans + mannans. Echinocandins hit glucan synthesis (wall); azoles/polyenes hit ergosterol (membrane).
5.Diagnosis pyramid: KOH/microscopy (fast, first-line, variable sensitivity) → Culture on SDA (most sensitive overall, slow) → Serology/PCR/MALDI-TOF/β-D-glucan (adjuncts for invasive disease).
6.MIC/CLSI breakpoints guide therapy, but most antifungals are fungistatic — susceptible ≠ guaranteed cure.
7.Malassezia furfur → tinea versicolor → hyper/hypopigmented trunk macules → "spaghetti and meatballs" KOH → selenium sulfide/azoles.
8.Hortaea werneckii → tinea nigra (dark palm/sole macule). Piedraia hortae → black piedra (hard/black). Trichosporon → white piedra (soft/yellow).
9.Three dermatophyte genera: Trichophyton (skin+hair+nails), Microsporum (skin+hair, no nails), Epidermophyton (skin+nails, no hair/no microconidia). Can't grow at 37°C → superficial only, but contagious.
10.Anthropophilic = mild/chronic, most human cases. Zoophilic/Geophilic = acute/inflammatory, may self-resolve.
11."Ringworm" = shape of lesion, not a worm. Ectothrix (outside hair, Microsporum, fluoresces green) vs. Endothrix (inside hair, T. tonsurans, no fluorescence). Severe capitis: Kerion (boggy) / Favus (crusts).
12.Tinea cruris with prominent scrotal involvement → think candidiasis, not tinea. Trichophytid reaction = hypersensitivity, not direct invasion.
13.Dermatophytosis treatment: topical (miconazole/tolnaftate/clotrimazole) for mild/localized, 2–4 wks; oral (griseofulvin/terbinafine/itraconazole) for extensive disease, tinea capitis, or tinea unguium.
14.All subcutaneous mycoses enter via traumatic inoculation from soil/plants; chronic, slow, granulomatous; systemic spread is rare.
15.Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix, dimorphic: mold 25°C / yeast 37°C): lymphocutaneous form (75%) → cord-like nodules. Hallmark = cigar-shaped yeast + asteroid bodies. Culture = gold standard (microscopy often falsely negative). Itraconazole = DOC.
16.Chromoblastomycosis (dematiaceous fungi): verrucous cauliflower-like lesion. Hallmark = muriform/sclerotic (Medlar/copper-penny) body on KOH. Surgery (small) / itraconazole or flucytosine (large). Relapse common.
17.Mycetoma: classic triad = swelling + draining sinuses + granules. White granules → Pseudallescheria boydii; black/red-black → Madurella/Exophiala. Eumycetoma = true fungi; actinomycetoma = bacteria (not covered here).
18.Video vs. Book trap: the lecture video and Jawetz swap the depth classification of Malassezia furfur and T. rubrum (superficial vs. cutaneous). This reviewer follows the book/main-trans convention.
19.Culture conditions: Yeasts 37°C, days. Molds 30°C, weeks. Dermatophyte culture: room temperature, ~1–3 weeks, on SDA/IMA ± cycloheximide/chloramphenicol.
20.Serology is not routinely recommended for sporotrichosis (poor sensitivity/specificity). Antigen serology (cryptococcal antigen, 1,3-beta-D-glucan) IS useful for invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis screening.
▶ Rapid-Fire Final Recall

Answer in a few words before tapping each card open.

What are the 4 classifications of mycoses by depth of invasion?
Superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous, systemic.
Of ~80,000 known fungal species, how many cause >90% of human infections?
Fewer than 50 species.
Which two fungi are commensal/endogenous rather than exogenous?
Dermatophytes and Candida.
Which immune responses are vital for fungal immunity?
Th1 and Th17.
Why is fungal virulence fundamentally different from bacterial virulence?
Fungi lack potent toxins — virulence instead comes from thermotolerance, enzyme secretion, and immune evasion.
What are the 3 main fungal cell wall polysaccharides?
Chitin, glucans, mannans.
Echinocandins vs. azoles/polyenes — which structure does each target?
Echinocandins → cell wall (β-glucan synthesis). Azoles/polyenes → cell membrane (ergosterol).
What is the first-line, rapid diagnostic test for fungal infection?
KOH prep (10–20%) microscopy.
Which stain gives fluorescent enhancement in fungal microscopy?
Calcofluor white.
What is the standard mycology culture medium?
Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA).
Which is more sensitive overall — culture or microscopy?
Culture (but it's slower).
What does MIC stand for, and which body sets the breakpoints?
Minimum inhibitory concentration; breakpoints set by CLSI.
Are most antifungal drugs fungistatic or fungicidal?
Fungistatic (they stop growth, not always kill).
What organism causes tinea (pityriasis) versicolor?
Malassezia furfur (also M. globosa, M. sympodialis).
Classic KOH description for Malassezia furfur?
"Spaghetti and meatballs."
What organism causes tinea nigra, and where does it classically appear?
Hortaea werneckii; dark macule on palms/soles.
What causes black piedra vs. white piedra?
Black = Piedraia hortae (hard). White = Trichosporon spp. (soft).
What are the three dermatophyte genera?
Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton.
Which genus skips the nails, and which skips the hair?
Microsporum skips nails; Epidermophyton skips hair.
Why can't dermatophytes cause deep or systemic infection?
They cannot grow at 37°C.
Which ecological category causes most human dermatophyte cases, and what pattern of disease?
Anthropophilic — mild, chronic, low-grade.
Does "ringworm" involve an actual worm?
No — it describes the ring-shaped lesion appearance.
Ectothrix or endothrix — which one fluoresces under Wood's lamp?
Ectothrix (arthroconidia outside the hair shaft).
Which organism is the classic example of endothrix tinea capitis?
Trichophyton tonsurans.
What are the two severe inflammatory forms of tinea capitis?
Kerion (boggy, painful) and Favus (yellow crusts/scutula).
Tinea cruris with prominent scrotal involvement should make you think of what instead?
Candidiasis.
Is a trichophytid reaction a direct fungal infection of the hands?
No — it's a hypersensitivity reaction to antigens from infection elsewhere.
Name three oral antifungals used for dermatophytosis.
Griseofulvin, terbinafine, itraconazole.
What genus causes sporotrichosis, and what is its thermal dimorphism pattern?
Sporothrix (schenckii complex) — mold at 25°C, yeast at 37°C.
Classic microscopic appearance of Sporothrix yeast cells, and what surrounds them in tissue?
Cigar-shaped budding yeast, surrounded by asteroid bodies.
What is the most common clinical form of sporotrichosis?
Lymphocutaneous (~75% of cases).
What is the gold standard for diagnosing sporotrichosis, and why does direct microscopy often fail?
Culture — direct microscopy is often negative because yeast cells are sparse in tissue.
What is the drug of choice for cutaneous/lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis?
Itraconazole.
What type of fungi causes chromoblastomycosis?
Dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi, e.g. Fonsecaea pedrosoi.
What is the key diagnostic tissue finding in chromoblastomycosis?
The muriform / sclerotic (Medlar, copper-penny) body.
Describe the classic clinical appearance of chromoblastomycosis.
Verrucous, cauliflower-like lesion.
What complication can chromoblastomycosis cause via lymphatic obstruction?
Elephantiasis.
What is the classic triad of mycetoma?
Localized swelling + draining sinuses/fistulae + granules.
White granules vs. black/red-black granules in mycetoma — which organisms do they suggest?
White → Pseudallescheria boydii. Black/red-black → Madurella or Exophiala.
What is the difference between eumycetoma and actinomycetoma?
Eumycetoma = true fungi. Actinomycetoma = filamentous bacteria (not covered in this lecture).
